title: Kyle Hansen, Ph.D.
text:
About Me

A Brief Bio
The Christian liberal arts have been a driving force throughout my life. My early education at Veritas School in Newberg, Oregon developed in my a passion for lifelong learning, which led me to study Mathematics and Computer Science at Westmont College. I graduated in 2019, and—inspired by a summer of research with Dr. Russell Howell—pursued a Ph.D. in Mathematics at UC Santa Barbara. Under the direction of my advisor, Dr. Fedya Manin, I studied how nilpotent algebraic structures influence both the geometric behavior of topological spaces, as well as the patterns of aperiodic tilings. I defended my thesis in 2025. That same fall, I returned with enthusiasm to Westmont College as an Assistant Professor of Mathematics. In my leisure time, I can be found singing, reading, swimming, biking, running, (or all three), baking, and enjoying the company of my church family.


Research Interests

Quantitative Topology
If you want to study the complexity of a topological space, you might study the algebraic invariants of this space. Often, however, topological spaces such as manifolds come equipped with some geometric structure as well. How does this algebraic topological complexity translate into geometric complexity? This broad question motivates the field of so-called “quantitative topology”.
For example, if you have a nullhomotopic map (a priori, algebraic information) into your space, what is the most efficient way to perform this nullhomotopy (geometric information)? My advisor Fedya Manin has asked (and answered) similar questions in the context of simpy connected target spaces, and some of my current work is an extension of this to nilpotent targets.
I have also studied elliptic manifolds, where I asked “Given a nilpotent Lie group \(G\), what algebraic information is necessary/sufficient to guarantee that a closed manifold \(M\) is \(G\)-elliptic?” In some sense, this asks which manifolds \(M\) can be efficiently wrapped using the group \(G\) as your wrapping paper. Recent advances in related areas have opened up some clear paths forward in this investigation, where it seems likely that the Heisenberg group is a poor choice of wrapping paper for a flat torus.


Tiling Spaces
I also study tiling spaces, where I am interested in extending some existing theory to the relevant nilpotent setting. For example, I extend work about the topology of Euclidean tiling spaces to tiling spaces of certain nilpotent Lie groups.

title: Policies
text:
God called us to co-create with Him as a part of our role in bearing His image. Collaboration—in which multiple people labor side-by-side towards a common goal—is a part of God’s good design for community and relationship. Learning communities function best when students have academic integrity. Cheating is primarily an offense against your classmates because it undermines our learning community. Therefore, dishonesty of any kind may result in loss of credit for the work involved and the filing of a report with the Provost’s Office. Major or repeated infractions may result in dismissal from the course with a grade of “F”. Be familiar with the College’s plagiarism policy, found at https://www.westmont.edu/office-provost/academic-program/academic-integrity-policy.
In particular, providing someone with an electronic copy of your work is a breach of the academic integrity policy. Do not email, post online, or otherwise disseminate any of the work that you do in this class. If you keep your work on a repository, make sure it is private. You may work with others on the assignments, but make sure that you write or type up your own answers yourself. You are on your honor that the work you hand in represents your own understanding.



Math courses will build your character by asking you to persevere through challenging problems. Such character is often built through practice. Any use of LLMs (etc.) that negate this practice will end up robbing you of your education. Moreover, you will naturally perform more poorly in this course as a result. Any unapproved use of LLMs (etc.) will constitute a breach of academic integrity.

title: Policies
text:
Accommodations and Accessability
Westmont is committed to ensuring equal access to academic courses and college programs. In keeping with this commitment under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA)of 1990, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, and the Americans with Disabilities Amendments Act (ADAAA) of 2008, individuals with diagnoses that impact major life activities are protected from discrimination and are entitled to reasonable accommodations. Students who choose to disclose a disability are encouraged to contact the Accessibility Resource Office (ARO) as early as possible in the semester to discuss potential accommodations for this course. Accommodations are designed to ensure equal access to programs for all students who have a disability that impacts their participation in college activities. Email aro@westmont.edu or see https://www.westmont.edu/accessibility-resources for more information.

title: Policies
text:
Assignments and Assessments

Formatting
Unless otherwise specified, all work should be handwritten (i.e., not typed up). Digital submissions will not be accepted except in rare, prearranged circumstances.


Credits & Collaborators
You may work with others on your assignments unless otherwise specified, but make sure that you write or type up your own answers yourself. You are on your honor that the work you hand in represents your own understanding. To maintain academic integrity, your work should list all people and resources you consulted while writing up your work.


Due Dates
All assignments and assessments must be turned in by the start of class on the day they are due. Work missed or turned in late (including tests) without a valid excuse will receive a zero, unless otherwise stated on the syllabus.

title: Policies
text:
Classroom Etiquette

Punctual Attendance
One of the primary resources you have in this class is the class time itself. If you miss a significant number of classes, you will almost definitely do poorly in this class. If you miss more than two weeks’ worth of classes without a valid excuse, I reserve the right to terminate you from the course with a failing grade.
Please be prepared to learn before the official start of class. Arriving late, or arriving without time to prepare yourself for class, distracts both myself and your peers. If such disruption becomes a habit, we will discuss practical methods of ensuring that class starts after you are prepared to begin. Arriving late to class constitutes a half day’s absence.


Entertainment Media
In his book “Amusing Ourselves to Death: Politics in the Age of Showbusiness” Neil Postman argues that technology whose primary vernacular is audio-visual will always present its content as “entertainment”. That is, television (and the screen-oriented media that permeate our modern era) naturally present objects as something whose purpose is amusement, rather than something worth investing thoughtful, patient, and prolonged engagement of one’s mind.
Mathematics is not amusing, nor should it be treated as such.
Starting from 5 minutes prior to class, until the end of the class period, I do not permit audio-visual media to be used in the classroom. Such media include (but are not limited to): cell phones, laptops, and tablets. For example, if class runs from 10:15-11:20am, cell phones may not be used between 10:10-11:20am while inside the classroom. This policy applies to myself. This policy may be adjusted in exceptional circumstances.

title: Lab Book
text:
What do you expect this blog post to be about? Seriously, take 10 seconds (no more) and make a guess.
It has been demonstrated1 that one is most effectively primed to learn new knowledge and information when one tries to make predictions about the new information to be received. This allows the brain to more readily find fitting connections for the new information to be slotted into the network of one’s pre-existing knowledge, solidifying old pathways while generating new ones. Later on, that connection (and the information itself) is solidified through the practice of retrieving the knowledge. This makes learning naturally into a three-act play.2


You might be familiar with this three-act structure in the form of lab reports, where you have a hypothesis, the experiment itself, and the results/discussion. Teaching is, in many ways, a continual experiement where none of the variables are held constant. Because this three-act structure is so widely used both as a way of building one’s knowledge, and for building on one’s knowledge through experimentation, I plan to implement a similar outline for evaluation of my classroom experiments as a teacher.
This blog, then, can be considered my personal lab book. In it, I intend to express my expectations, my decisions, and my reactions/reflections throughout my teaching career. Because my own new learning will be interwoven with these stages, other notes and reflections on various readings/ideas will likely be strewn about as well.3



If this blog is a lab book, this post is the introduction to my first attempt at keeping a lab book. In it, I intend to set the stage for how I expect to maintain this lab book throughout the upcoming term, and (perhaps) beyond. This is a meta-post, in the sense that it is itself a preview of my experimental method; later, I should end up making some meta-notes about the experiment of this experimental method, and after that, review some of the things that wend well and what went poorly, and how to revise my method.4

text:
The Experiment
This upcoming term, I plan to implement three phases to the experiment of my teaching. I will call these three stages the PRE-views, the INTER-views, and the RE-views of the term.5
I hit the point of diminishing returns a while ago, and should have stopped writing like…an hour ago. I’m still learning to stop before that happens. Whoops. I’ll get to writing this tomorrow. or the next day.
20-ish hours later
I’m now returning to this blog post. I’m trying to implement active approaches to stopping early, before diminishing returns set in6 on work projects. This might mean leaving some ideas unfinished, and returning to them at a later time, working in brief regular sessions to lower the barrier to re-entry.7 I failed at this yesterday, but I’m back.
I expect this blog itself to provide me opportunities for breif, regular sessions8 of preparation and reflection as I process my teaching, research, and service as a professor. In the rest of this section, I outline some of my current working philosophy behind the three-act structure (PRE-, INTER-, and RE-views) I expect my notes to take.

PREviews
Influenced by past reviews, aimed at future interviews, I plan to implement previews as a method of laying out plans and predictions for upcoming terms, units, lectures, projects, etc. Ideally, every “large-scale” item (e.g., each semester and/or new course preps, research projects, service endeavor) will begin with me making plans and predictions about that project. This is where I will break down the larger task into what I predict will be smaller-scale items, and why I made the decisions that I did. These smaller items may also possibly merit their own subjection to the pre-, inter-, re-view structure, but often they will be independently processed through “interviews”.


INTERviews
Influenced by past previews, aimed at future reviews, I plan to conduct interviews as a way of touching base on the core elements of a larger project. This is where I will record how I approached specific events, the events that actually transpired, and my (near-immediate) reflections on the outcomes. I call these “inter”views not only to keep with the “__view” theme, but also to remind myself that this is a time to ask and answer questions about the events that transpired, and how they relate to the project at large. Sometimes, these “inter”views may seem more like public journal entries, and I’m kind of okay with that. I will not use identifying student information, and will not stories involving students without their express permission. Eventually, my responses will be compiled at a larger scale on a given project in “reviews”.


REviews
Influenced by past interviews, aimed at informing future previews, I plan to conduct reviews as a systematic way of processing both my predictions and reactions to events, and summarizing some of my strengths, weaknesses, continued questions, new ideas, etc. in order to grow in the future. I hope these reviews eventually become useful tools for my own compilation into P/R/T documents, and provide a little peek into how I process the events of my classroom.
